source_text: OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram, verecundius ac melius existimans errantis imperitiam silentio spernere, quam loquendo dementis insaniam provocare. Nec hoc sine magisterii divini auctoritate faciebam, cum scriptum sit: In aures imprudentis noli quicquam dicere, ne, quando audierit, irrideat sensatos sermones tuos. Et iterum: Noli respondere imprudenti ad imprudentiam ejus, ne similis fias illi. Et sanctum quoque jubeamur intra conscientiam nostram tenere, nec inculcandum porcis et canibus exponere, loquente Domino et dicente: Ne dederitis sanctum canibus, neque miseritis margaritas vestras ante porcos, ne inculcent eas pedibus, et conversi elidant vos. Nam, cum ad me saepe, studio magis contradicendi quam voto discendi, venires, et, clamosis vocibus personans, malles tua impudenter ingerere quam nostra patienter audire, ineptum videbatur congredi tecum, quando facilius esset et levius turbulenti maris concitos fluctus clamoribus retundere quam tuam rabiem tractatibus coercere. Certe et labor irritus et nullus effectus, offerre lumen caeco, sermonem surdo, sapientiam bruto; cum nec sentire brutus possit, nec caecus lumen admittere, nec surdus audire. Haec considerans, saepe conticui, et impatientem patientia vici, cum nec docere indocilem possem, nec impium religione comprimere, nec furentem lenitate cohibere. Sed enim, cum dicas plurimos conqueri quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames saeviant, quodque imbres et pluvias serena longa suspendant nobis imputari, tacere ultra non oportet; ne jam non verecundiae sed diffidentiae esse incipiat quod tacemus, et dum criminationes falsas contemnimus refutare, videamur crimen agnoscere. Respondeo igitur et tibi, Demetriane, pariter et caeteris quos tu forsitan concitasti, et adversum nos odia tuis maledicis vocibus seminando, comites tibi plures radicis atque originis tuae pullulatione fecisti; quos tamen sermonis nostri admittere credo rationem: nam qui ad malum motus est mendacio fallente, multo magis ad bonum movebitur veritate cogente. Dixisti per nos fieri et quod nobis debeant imputari omnia ista quibus nunc mundus quatitur et urgetur, quod dii vestri a nobis non colantur. Qua in parte, quia ignarus divinae cognitionis et veritatis alienus es, illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam mundum, non illis viribus stare quibus prius steterat, nec vigore et robore eo valere quo antea praevalebat. Hoc etiam, nobis tacentibus et nulla de Scripturis sanctis praedicationibusque divinis documenta promentibus, mundus ipse jam loquitur et occasum sui rerum labentium probatione testatur. Non hyeme nutriendis seminibus tanta imbrium copia est, non frugibus aestate torrendis solis tanta flagrantia est, nec sic vernante temperie sata laeta sunt, nec adeo arboreis foetibus autumna foecunda sunt. Minus de effossis et fatigatis montibus eruuntur marmorum crustae, minus argenti et auri opes suggerunt exhausta jam metalla, et pauperes venae breviantur in dies singulos et decrescunt, deficit in arvis agricola, in mari nauta, miles in castris, innocentia in foro, justitia in judicio, in amicitiis concordia, in artibus peritia, in moribus disciplina. Putasne tantam posse substantiam rei senescentis existere quantum prius potuit novellu adhuc et vegeta juventa pollere? Minuatur necesse est quicquid fine jam proximo in occidua et extrema devergit. Sic sol in occasu suo radios minus claro et igneo splendore jaculatur; sic, declinante jam cursu, exoletis cornibus luna tenuatur, et arbor quae fuerat ante viridis et fertilis, arescentibus ramis fit postmodum sterili senectute deformis; et fons qui, exundantibus prius venis, largiter profluebat, senectute deficiens, vix modico sudore distillat. Haec sententia mundo data est, haec Dei lex est, ut omnia orta occidant et aucta senescant, et infirmentur fortia, et magna minuantur, et cum infirmata et diminuta fuerint, finiantur. Christianis imputas quod minuantur singula, mundo senescente. Quid si et senes imputent Christianis quod minus valeant in senectute, quod non perinde ut prius vigeant auditu aurium, cursu pedum, oculorum acie, virium robore, succo viscerum, mole membrorum; et cum olim ultra octingentos et nongentos annos vita hominum longaeva procederet, vix nunc possit ad centenarium numerum perveniri? Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt antequam crescant; nec aetas in senectute desinit, sed incipit a senectute. Sic in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat; sic quodcumque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat: ut nemo mirari debeat singula in mundo coepisse deficere, quando totus ipse jam mundus in defectione sit et in fine.
pass_a_gloss: I had often despised you, Demetrianus, speaking against God, who is one and true, with sacrilegious mouth and impious words, considering it more decent and better to scorn the ignorance of the erring in silence, rather than to provoke the madness of the demented by speaking. And I did not do this without the authority of divine teaching, since it is written: Do not say anything in the ears of the imprudent, lest, when he hears, he ridicules your sensible words. And again: Do not respond to the imprudent according to his imprudence, lest you become like him. We are also commanded to keep the holy within our conscience, and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, speaking and saying: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. For when you came to me often, more with the intention of contradicting than of learning, and, with loud voices, preferred to impudently impose your own thoughts rather than patiently listen to ours, it seemed foolish to engage with you, since it would be easier and less troublesome to calm the turbulent waves of a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your rage with discussions. Certainly, it is a labor in vain and without effect to offer light to the blind, speech to the deaf, wisdom to the brute; since the brute cannot perceive, the blind cannot admit light, and the deaf cannot hear. Considering these things, I often kept silent, and overcame the impatient with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable, nor restrain the impious with religion, nor calm the raging with gentleness. But since you say that many complain that wars arise more frequently, that plagues, that famines rage, that rains and showers suspend the long periods of fair weather for us, it is not fitting to remain silent any longer; lest what we keep silent about begin not to be out of modesty but out of diffidence, and while we disdain to refute false accusations, we seem to acknowledge the crime. I respond, therefore, to you, Demetrianus, and to the others whom you may have stirred up, and who, with your slanderous voices, have sown hatred against us, and have made many companions for yourself from the root and origin of your own multitude; whom, however, I believe will admit the reason of our words: for he who is moved to evil by deceitful falsehood, will be moved much more to good by compelling truth. You said that through us these things happen, and that all these things, by which the world is now shaken and pressed, should be imputed to us, because your gods are not worshiped by us. In this part, since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and alien to truth, you should first know that the world has already grown old, does not stand with the same strength as before, and does not prevail with the same vigor and robustness as it once did. This the world itself now says, even if we are silent and do not produce any documents from the holy Scriptures and divine preachings, and the proof of its declining things testifies to its own downfall. There is not such an abundance of rains to nourish the seeds in winter, not such heat of the sun to scorch the crops in summer, nor are the sown things so joyful in the spring, nor is autumn so fertile with tree fruits. Less and less marble is extracted from the excavated and exhausted mountains, less and less wealth of silver and gold is produced, since the metals are now exhausted, and the poor veins are shortened day by day and decrease, the farmer fails in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp, innocence in the forum, justice in judgment, concord in friendships, skill in arts, discipline in morals. Do you think that such a great substance of a thing that is growing old can exist as it once could when it was still new and flourishing in its youth? It is necessary that whatever is already near its end and is declining into old age and extreme weakness be diminished. Thus, the sun, in its setting, throws its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus, with its course already declining, the moon is diminished with worn-out horns, and the tree, which was once green and fertile, becomes sterile and deformed in its old age, with withering branches; and the spring, which once flowed abundantly, with its veins now failing in old age, barely trickles with a small sweat. This sentence has been given to the world, this is the law of God, that all things that have arisen will decline, and all things that have grown will grow old, and the strong will be weakened, and the great will be diminished, and when they have been weakened and diminished, they will come to an end. You impute to Christians that individual things are diminishing, because the world is growing old. What if the old also impute to Christians that they are less strong in old age, that they do not thrive as much as before in hearing, in the running of feet, in the sharpness of eyes, in the robustness of strength, in the moisture of viscera, in the mass of limbs; and whereas human life once lasted beyond eight hundred and nine hundred years, it can now hardly reach the number of a hundred? We see gray hair in children, hair is lacking before it grows; nor does age end in old age, but begins with old age. Thus, in its very birth, nativity hastens to its end; thus, whatever is now born, degenerates because of the old age of the world itself: so that no one should wonder that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world itself is already in decline and at its end.

pass_b_english: I have often held you in contempt, Demetrianus, because you blaspheme the one true God with a sacrilegious mouth and impious words. I judged it more decent and better to scorn the ignorance of the erring in silence than to provoke the madness of the demented by speaking. I did not do this on my own authority, but on that of divine teaching, for it is written: "Do not speak to a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words" (Proverbs 9:7-8), and again: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself" (Proverbs 26:4). We are also commanded to keep what is holy within our conscience and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, as the Lord says: "Do not give what is holy to dogs; do not throw your pearls to pigs, or they will trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces" (Matthew 7:6). You came to me often, more intent on contradicting than on learning, and with loud voices you insisted on imposing your own views impudently rather than listening to ours patiently. Engaging with you seemed pointless, since it would be easier to calm a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your rage with discussion. Offering light to the blind, speech to the deaf, or wisdom to a brute is labor in vain and without effect; a brute cannot perceive, the blind cannot receive light, and the deaf cannot hear. Weighing this, I often kept silent and overcame your impatience with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable, nor restrain the impious by religion, nor calm the raging with gentleness.

But now you claim that many complain of wars breaking out more frequently, of plagues and famines raging, and of long droughts withholding rain — and you blame us because your gods are no longer worshiped. I can no longer stay silent, lest my silence look not like modesty but like diffidence, and lest my refusal to refute false charges seem like an admission of guilt. So I answer you, Demetrianus, and the others you have stirred up with your slanderous voices, sowing hatred against us and gathering a crowd from the root and stock of your own kind. Yet I believe they will accept the reason of our words, for whoever is driven to evil by deceit will be driven even more powerfully to good by compelling truth.

You say these disasters happen through us and should be imputed to us because we do not worship your gods. Since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and a stranger to the truth, you must first understand this: the world has grown old. It no longer stands with the strength it once had, nor does it thrive with its former vigor. Even without our testimony from Scripture or divine preaching, the world itself testifies to its own decline. Winter rains no longer nourish the seed abundantly; summer sun no longer ripens the crops with such heat; spring sowings are no longer so joyful; autumn harvests are no longer so rich in fruit. Less marble is quarried from exhausted mountains; less silver and gold are mined, for the veins are spent and dwindle daily. The farmer fails in the field, the sailor at sea, the soldier in camp; innocence fails in the forum, justice in the courts, concord among friends, skill in the arts, discipline in morals. Do you think a thing grown old can retain the substance it had when it was new and flourishing? Whatever nears its end and declines into extreme old age must diminish. The setting sun casts its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; the waning moon shrinks with worn horns; a tree once green and fertile becomes sterile and deformed in old age, its branches withering; a spring that once flowed abundantly now barely trickles as its veins fail. This is the sentence given to the world, this is the law of God: all that has arisen will decline, all that has grown will age, the strong will be weakened, the great diminished, and when weakened and diminished, they will end.

You blame Christians for the diminishing of individual things in an aging world. What if the old blamed Christians for their own failing strength — for hearing, running, eyesight, vigor, moisture, and mass not holding as they once did? Human life once exceeded eight or nine hundred years; now it scarcely reaches a hundred. We see gray hair on children; hair falls out before it grows. Age does not end in old age — it begins with it. From its very birth, nativity hastens to its end; whatever is born now degenerates because the world itself is old. No one should wonder that individual things in the world begin to fail when the whole world is already in decline and at its end.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Scripture citations in Pass B (Proverbs 9:7-8, Proverbs 26:4, Matthew 7:6) correctly identify the content of the Latin quotes. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source and each other.
